section.title: Laws of Restitution and Justice
section.sectionRationale: This chapter continues the Book of the Covenant's case law into property, negligence, sexual ethics, and social justice, closing with some of the Torah's most tender commands: do not oppress the foreigner, the widow, or the orphan, for the LORD Himself hears their cry.
section.thesis: The LORD legislates fair restitution for theft and property damage, protects the vulnerable, the foreigner, widow, orphan, and poor, from exploitation, and calls Israel to be a holy people whose ordinary economic and social life reflects the character of the God who redeemed them from Egypt.
section.frameNote: Five movements: laws of theft and restitution; property damage and disputes over safekeeping; sexual ethics and capital offenses against exclusive worship; tender protections for the foreigner, widow, orphan, and poor; and closing instructions on holiness in ordinary obligations.

verses.text: “If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters or sells it, he must {{repay|repay}} five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep.
If a thief is caught breaking in and is beaten to death, no one shall be guilty of bloodshed.

But if it happens after sunrise, there is guilt for his bloodshed. 
A thief must make full restitution; if he has nothing, he himself shall be sold for his theft.
If what was stolen is actually found alive in his possession, whether ox or donkey or sheep, he must pay back double.
If a man grazes his livestock in a field or vineyard and allows them to stray so that they graze in someone else's field, he must make restitution from the best of his own field or vineyard.
If a fire breaks out and spreads to thornbushes so that it consumes stacked or standing grain, or the whole field, the one who started the fire must make full restitution.
If a man gives his neighbor money or goods for safekeeping and they are stolen from the neighbor's house, the thief, if caught, must pay back double.
If the thief is not found, the owner of the house must appear before the judges to determine whether he has taken his neighbor's property.

In all cases of illegal possession of an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a garment, or any lost item that someone claims, ‘This is mine,’ both parties shall bring their cases before the judges. The one whom the judges find guilty must pay back double to his neighbor.
If a man gives a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any other animal to be cared for by his neighbor, but it dies or is injured or stolen while no one is watching,
an oath before the LORD shall be made between the parties to determine whether or not the man has taken his neighbor's property. The owner must accept the oath and require no restitution.
But if the animal was actually stolen from the neighbor, he must make restitution to the owner.
If the animal was torn to pieces, he shall bring it as evidence; he need not make restitution for the torn carcass.
If a man borrows an animal from his neighbor and it is injured or dies while its owner is not present, he must make full restitution.
If the owner was present, no restitution is required. If the animal was rented, the fee covers the loss.
If a man seduces a virgin who is not pledged in marriage and sleeps with her, he must pay the full dowry for her to be his wife.
If her father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the man still must pay an amount comparable to the bridal price of a virgin.
You must not allow a sorceress to live.
Whoever lies with an animal must surely be put to death.
If anyone sacrifices to any god other than the LORD alone, he must be set apart for destruction.

units.label: The foreigner, the widow, the orphan
units.note: I will surely hear their cry

verses.text: You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.
You must not mistreat any widow or orphan.
If you do mistreat them, and they {{cry|cry out}} to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry.
My anger will be kindled, and I will kill you with the sword; then your wives will become widows and your children will be fatherless.
If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest.
If you take your neighbor's cloak as collateral, return it to him by sunset,
because his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in? And if he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.

units.label: Holiness in ordinary obligations
units.note: you are to be My holy people

verses.text: You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people.
You must not hold back offerings from your granaries or vats. You are to give Me the firstborn of your sons.
You shall do likewise with your cattle and your sheep. Let them stay with their mothers for seven days, but on the eighth day you are to give them to Me.
You are to be My {{holy|holy}} people. You must not eat the meat of a mauled animal found in the field; you are to throw it to the dogs.

repay.gloss: To repay, restore, make whole, from the same root as shalom, peace. Restitution in Israel's law is never merely punitive; it is meant to restore what was broken and make the wronged party whole again.

cry.gloss: To cry out in distress, the same word used of Israel's own cry under Egyptian oppression, Exodus 3:7. God warns that the vulnerable person's cry reaches Him exactly as Israel's own cry once did, and He will act the same way in response.

holy.gloss: Holy, set apart, belonging distinctly to God. This closing command ties even the most mundane obligations, dietary rules, offerings, restitution, to Israel's fundamental identity as a people set apart to reflect God's own character.

basic.context: This chapter continues Israel's case law: how to make restitution for theft, how to settle disputes over borrowed or lost property, and firm penalties for serious sins. It closes with some of the most tender laws in the whole Torah, protecting foreigners, widows, orphans, and the poor from exploitation.
basic.hermeneutics: These are specific civil and case laws for ancient Israel's courts, not a direct legal code for governments today. Their enduring value is the moral principle underneath: restitution restores rather than merely punishes, and God cares fiercely for the powerless, principles fulfilled and deepened rather than abolished in the new covenant.
basic.originalLanguages: Restitution in this chapter is called shalam, to make whole, sharing a root with shalom, peace, restoring wholeness rather than merely inflicting pain. God warns that if the vulnerable tsa'aq, cry out, in distress, He will hear them exactly as He heard Israel's own cry in Egypt. And the whole chapter closes by calling Israel qadosh, holy, set apart in every corner of ordinary life.
basic.typology: The double restitution required of a thief anticipates the far greater restitution Christ makes, not merely restoring what was lost but giving abundantly more, life to the full, in the place of what sin destroyed.
basic.christ: Zacchaeus's spontaneous promise to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated, Luke 19:8, directly echoes this chapter's restitution laws, showing repentance in Christ working itself out in concrete, costly justice. And Jesus, who had no place to lay His head, embodies the same compassion this law commands toward the poor stranger with nothing to his name.
basic.god: God is meticulously just, insisting wrongs be made right down to the smallest detail of property and dispute, and He is fiercely compassionate, promising personal, furious intervention on behalf of anyone who exploits the widow, orphan, or foreigner. His justice and His tenderness toward the powerless are never separated.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 19:8-9 shows Zacchaeus applying this same principle of fourfold restitution after meeting Christ. James 1:27 defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows, echoing this chapter directly. Deuteronomy 10:18-19 grounds Israel's care for the foreigner in the same memory of Egypt.
basic.oneStory: God builds justice and compassion into the smallest details of Israel's civil life, insisting that restitution restore what was broken and that the powerless never be exploited. This concern for the vulnerable and for genuine restitution runs through the whole Bible and finds its fullest expression in Christ, who restores far more than was ever lost.

context.literary:
Exodus 22 continues the Book of the Covenant without a pause. Hebrew Bibles in fact number its first verse as the last verse of chapter 21, so that the theft of an ox follows directly on the goring ox. The chapter falls into two halves that differ in voice. Verses 1 to 17 keep the case form of chapter 21, "If a man... then...," dealing with theft, damage, deposits, borrowed animals and seduction. From verse 18 the form changes to direct command, "You must not...," and the subject widens from the courtroom to the whole of Israel's life before God.

The first half is held together by a single refrain. Forms of the verb for making restitution run through verses 1 to 15 again and again, and the phrase "pay back double" marks verses 4, 7 and 9. The law is teaching Israel to ask one question of every loss: what will make this whole?

The second half rises in intensity and then turns tender. Three capital offences in verses 18 to 20 guard Israel's exclusive bond with the LORD: sorcery, bestiality and sacrifice to other gods. Then, with no break, come the foreigner, the widow, the orphan and the borrower, verses 21 to 27. Here the law speaks with emotion found in few legal texts anywhere. God reasons with Israel ("What else will he sleep in?"), threatens those who abuse the weak, and describes Himself: "I am compassionate," verse 27.

Verses 28 to 31 close the unit by returning to God's claims: His name and His appointed ruler are not to be cursed, His share of harvest and firstborn is not to be withheld, and His people are to be holy even in what they eat. The chapter thus moves from the barnyard to the sanctuary, and the final word, "You are to be My holy people," verse 31, gathers all of it into one identity.
context.historical:
The world of this chapter is a village of farmers and herders. Wealth was counted in oxen, sheep and donkeys, grain was stacked in the open field, and a spark in dry thornbushes could destroy a year's harvest, verse 6. There were no banks, so people left money or goods with a neighbour for safekeeping, verse 7, and a herdsman might pasture another man's animals for a season, verse 10. Jacob's complaint to Laban, "I did not bring you anything torn by wild beasts; I bore the loss myself," Genesis 31:39, shows how contested such arrangements could be. Exodus 22:13 protects the herdsman who can show the torn remains, as Amos 3:12 pictures a shepherd snatching "two legs or a piece of an ear" from a lion.

Houses were often built of mud brick, and a thief could dig through the wall at night. The law distinguishes the night intruder, whom a householder cannot see or judge, from the daylight thief, whom he could identify and take to court, verses 2 to 3. A thief who could not repay was sold into servitude to cover the loss, which links this chapter to the servant laws of 21:2.

The marriage customs of verses 16 to 17 assume the mohar, the bride price paid by a groom to the bride's family, as Shechem offered in Genesis 34:12 and Saul demanded of David in 1 Samuel 18:25. A seduced daughter's prospects of marriage were gravely damaged, so the man was required to marry her or pay the full price.

The poor of verses 25 to 27 were typically small farmers in a bad year, borrowing seed or food to survive. A cloak was often the only pledge they had, and it doubled as their bedding. Among Israel's neighbours interest on loans of grain and silver was normal and often steep. Israel was to lend to its poor without it.
context.canonical:
The restitution laws echo through Israel's story. When Nathan told David of the rich man who took a poor man's lamb, the king answered from this chapter: "he must pay for the lamb four times over," 2 Samuel 12:6, not knowing he was pronouncing his own sentence. Proverbs 6:30-31 speaks of a thief who must pay sevenfold. Zacchaeus reaches for the same law in Luke 19:8, and Paul turns it into a new calling: the one who has been stealing "must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need," Ephesians 4:28.

The protection of the foreigner, widow and orphan becomes one of the great refrains of the Old Testament. Leviticus 19:33-34 commands Israel to "love him as yourself," and Deuteronomy 10:17-19 grounds it in God's own character: He "executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner." The Psalms praise Him as "a father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows," Psalm 68:5. The prophets use the same triad as the test of Israel's faithfulness, Isaiah 1:17 and 1:23, Zechariah 7:10, Malachi 3:5. Amos condemns those who "lie down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge," Amos 2:8, a direct breach of verses 26 to 27, and Nehemiah rebukes the nobles for "exacting usury from your own brothers," Nehemiah 5:7.

In the New Testament Paul quotes verse 28 when he realises he has spoken sharply to the high priest: "Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people," Acts 23:5. Jesus condemns those who "defraud widows of their houses," Mark 12:40, and tells of a widow who cries for justice until she is heard, Luke 18:1-8. James defines pure religion as care for orphans and widows, James 1:27, and warns rich landowners that the cries of cheated workers "have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts," James 5:4. The call to be a holy people, verse 31, is taken up for the church in 1 Peter 2:9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to see that the God who redeemed them cares about what happens in the field, the barn and the moneylender's house as much as at the altar. The first half of the chapter teaches that wrongdoing creates a debt that must be paid to the person wronged. Justice is not satisfied when the thief is merely hurt; it is satisfied when the victim is restored, and when the thief pays more than he took, so that stealing never pays.

The second half teaches that power over the weak is held under God's eye. The foreigner, the widow, the orphan and the debtor had no one to speak for them in court. God announces that He Himself will hear them, and He reminds Israel that they once stood in exactly that place: "you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt," verse 21. Memory of their own redemption was meant to become mercy toward others.

Finally, the closing verses tie it all to holiness. A people set apart to God must be different in their loyalties (no sorcery, no other gods), in their speech (no cursing God or the ruler), in their giving (no holding back firstfruits) and even in their eating. Moses wanted Israel to grasp that holiness is not only a matter of the sanctuary; it reaches into every transaction.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These were binding civil and religious laws for Israel under the Sinai covenant. Their penalties, including the death sentences of verses 18 to 20, belonged to a nation in which the LORD was King and the covenant was the constitution. The New Testament does not hand those penalties to the church or to modern states; it answers the same sins with church discipline, repentance and the gospel, as when the Ephesian believers burned their books of magic, Acts 19:18-19.

What carries forward directly is the moral pattern. Restitution is still part of repentance, as Zacchaeus shows, Luke 19:8. Care for the foreigner, widow and orphan is still the test of true religion, James 1:27. Lending to the poor is still to be marked by mercy rather than profit, and Jesus pushes it further: "lend to them, expecting nothing in return," Luke 6:35. The call to holiness in ordinary life is repeated almost word for word: "be holy in all you do," 1 Peter 1:15. The specific rules about dowries, torn carcasses and grazing animals apply their principle to Israel's world, and Christians apply the same principle to their own.

debates.question: How should the death penalty prescribed for sorcery, bestiality, and idolatry in verses 18 to 20 be understood today?

views.label: Civil law specific to Israel's theocratic nationhood
views.case: These offenses directly threatened Israel's covenant identity as a nation uniquely bound to the LORD; the civil penalty was tied to Israel's specific national calling and boundary-keeping, not a universal template for civil governments.

views.label: Reflecting the seriousness of the underlying sin, even where the civil penalty does not carry over
views.case: While the death penalty itself belonged to Israel's old covenant civil law and does not bind modern civil authorities or the church, the severity reflects how seriously God regards occult practice, idolatry, and sexual perversion, sins the New Testament continues to name gravely even without prescribing the same civil punishment, 1 Corinthians 6:9-11, Galatians 5:19-21.

debates.bearing: Both views agree the civil penalty was specific to Israel's covenant nationhood and does not directly apply today; the underlying moral seriousness of these sins, however, remains, addressed now through church discipline and gospel transformation rather than civil execution.

debates.question: Does the ban on interest in 22:25 forbid all lending at interest, or only exploiting the poor?

views.label: A ban on all interest between fellow believers
views.case: Leviticus 25:36-37 and Deuteronomy 23:19 forbid charging a brother interest on any kind of loan, and the Psalms praise the one 'who lends his money without interest,' Psalm 15:5. For much of church history, from the church fathers through the medieval period, lending at interest was treated as sinful usury for Christians.

views.label: A protection for the poor, not a ban on commercial credit
views.case: Exodus 22:25 is framed around lending to 'one of My people among you who is poor,' and Leviticus 25:35-37 concerns a countryman who has become destitute. On this reading the law forbids profiting from another's desperation, not investment in trade. Calvin and many of the Reformers took this line, permitting moderate interest in commerce while forbidding it on loans to the needy. Jesus' parable assumes interest from bankers without condemning it, Matthew 25:27.

debates.bearing: The text itself sets the loan in the context of poverty and the pledge of a cloak, so its first concern is clearly the desperate borrower. Whatever one concludes about commercial lending, the passage forbids making money out of another person's crisis and calls believers to lend to the needy as God has dealt with them.

study.originalLanguages:
The night burglar of verse 2 is caught bammachteret, literally "in the digging through," from a root meaning to dig. Houses of mud brick could be tunnelled, and Jeremiah 2:34 uses the same noun for "breaking in." Jesus' warnings about thieves who "break in," Matthew 6:19 and 24:43, use a Greek verb that also means "dig through." The ruling that "no one shall be guilty of bloodshed" is literally "there is no blood for him," that is, no blood guilt falls on the householder; after sunrise "there is blood for him," and the thief's life counts again.

In verses 8 and 9 the disputing parties come "before the judges," but the Hebrew is ha'elohim, as the footnote notes, "before God." Verse 9 then says "the one whom the judges find guilty," where the verb is plural with elohim as its subject, and the footnote offers "whom God condemns." The cases were probably heard at a sanctuary, and God's verdict was sought through the oath of verse 11. Either way, the court was understood to sit under God's authority.

The torn animal of verse 13 is tarof yittaref, "surely torn," and the "mauled animal" of verse 31 is terefah from the same root. The two uses frame the chapter: one excuses a herdsman, the other defines what a holy people may not eat. Leviticus 17:15 and Ezekiel 44:31 take up the same word.

The seducer of verse 16 is one who "entices," from patah, the root behind the "simple," easily persuaded person of Proverbs. Jeremiah uses the same verb when he complains, "You have deceived me, O LORD," Jeremiah 20:7. The law treats seduction as persuasion that exploits, and it places the cost on the man.

Verse 18 literally says "a sorceress you shall not let live," putting the object first for emphasis, and verse 20 uses the verb charam, "be set apart for destruction," which the footnote explains as giving something over to the LORD by destroying it. The same word governs Jericho in Joshua 6:17. The one who gives himself to other gods is himself given over.

The protection of the weak is built with the vocabulary of Egypt. "Oppress" in verse 21 is lachats, the very word of Exodus 3:9, "I have seen how severely the Egyptians are oppressing them." "Mistreat" in verses 22 and 23 is innah, the verb of Exodus 1:11-12, where Egypt "oppressed" Israel with forced labour. Verse 23 then piles up three doubled verbs in a row: literally, "if you surely afflict him, if he surely cries to Me, I will surely hear his cry." The emphasis is unmistakable.

"Interest" in verse 25 is neshekh, a noun from a verb meaning to bite, and the one who must not "act as a creditor" is the moneylender who presses for repayment. "I am compassionate" in verse 27 is channun, better known as "gracious," the word that stands in God's own self-description in Exodus 34:6. Finally, "You are to be My holy people" in verse 31 is literally "men of holiness you shall be to Me," with the emphasis on God's ownership: they are holy because they are His.

typology.type: Restitution paid by one who did not steal, Exodus 22:1-4
typology.fulfillment: The law required the thief to repay more than he had taken. Psalm 69:4, a psalm the New Testament applies to Jesus more than once, has the righteous sufferer say, "Though I did not steal, I must repay." The correspondence is striking: at the cross the innocent One makes restitution for what others took from God, His glory and His due. The escalation is that the one who pays is not the guilty party at all, and the payment is His own life. The type falls short because the thief of Exodus 22 paid for his own theft; Christ paid for ours, and He restores us not fourfold but into the very riches of God, 2 Corinthians 8:9.

typology.type: The thief sold for a debt he cannot pay, Exodus 22:3
typology.fulfillment: A thief with nothing was sold into servitude to cover his debt. Jesus tells of a servant whose master "ordered that he be sold to pay his debt, along with his wife and children," and who was then forgiven and released out of compassion, Matthew 18:25-27. Paul says that God "canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us," nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:14. The law's pattern of a debt that must be paid stays in place; the escalation is that God Himself pays it. The type falls short in that the Hebrew debtor worked his way free, while no sinner can.

typology.type: The firstborn given to God, Exodus 22:29-30
typology.fulfillment: Israel's firstborn sons belonged to God because He spared them when Egypt's firstborn died, Exodus 13:14-15, and they were redeemed with a price. Jesus as the firstborn was presented at the temple "as it is written in the Law of the Lord," Luke 2:22-23. Yet the Father did not redeem His own firstborn; He "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all," Romans 8:32. That is the escalation: Israel's sons were bought back, while God's Son was given so that many could become "the congregation of the firstborn," Hebrews 12:23, and He the "firstborn among many brothers," Romans 8:29.

typology.type: God who hears the cry of the widow and the orphan, Exodus 22:22-23
typology.fulfillment: The LORD promised to hear personally when the widow and orphan cried out. In Jesus that promise takes flesh. At Nain He met a funeral procession for "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow," and "He had compassion on her," raised the young man, and "gave him back to his mother," Luke 7:12-15. The God who threatened in Exodus 22:24 to make oppressors' wives into widows here turns a widow's grief into joy. The type is not an empty picture but a direct continuity: the one who hears is the same God, now present among the poor.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through its central idea, restitution. The law insists that loss be made good, and more than good. Psalm 69, which the Gospels and Paul apply to Jesus, contains the line "Though I did not steal, I must repay," Psalm 69:4. At the cross the one person who had taken nothing from anyone makes good what humanity had stolen from God. He is crucified between two criminals, Luke 23:32-33, treated as a thief so that thieves could be restored. Jesus draws the contrast Himself: "The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness," John 10:10.

It leads to Christ through the poor man's cloak. God forbids keeping a debtor's cloak overnight: "What else will he sleep in?" verse 27. At Golgotha the soldiers divided Jesus' garments and gambled for His tunic, John 19:23-24. The one who would clothe His people in righteousness allowed Himself to be stripped of the last thing He had. Paul sums it up: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich," 2 Corinthians 8:9.

It leads to Christ through the foreigner. Israel was told to love the foreigner because they had been foreigners. Jesus identifies Himself with the stranger: "I was a stranger and you took Me in," Matthew 25:35, and He makes the treatment of "the least of these" the measure of love for Him, Matthew 25:40. Through Him those who were once outsiders become "fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household," Ephesians 2:19, while the church itself lives as "foreigners and exiles" in the world, 1 Peter 2:11, and so must never forget the foreigner.

It leads to Christ through the God who hears. The triple emphasis of verse 23, "I will surely hear," is fulfilled when the Lord sees a grieving widow at Nain and has compassion, Luke 7:13. Jesus teaches His disciples to pray like the widow who kept crying out, assuring them that God "will promptly carry out justice on their behalf," Luke 18:7-8.

It leads to Christ through the firstborn. Every firstborn son belonged to God, verse 29, and Jesus was presented in fulfilment of that law, Luke 2:22-23. But where Israel's sons were redeemed, God gave His own Son, Romans 8:32.

A caution: the chapter's rules about fire, deposits and grazing are not hidden pictures of the gospel. They are real law for real neighbours. The links to Christ come through the themes the chapter itself makes central, restitution, compassion for the weak, a God who hears, and a people made holy, and through the New Testament's own use of them.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is the God of the ordinary. He speaks about stray cattle, grass fires, borrowed donkeys and broken walls. Nothing is too small to fall under His justice, because every loss belongs to a person made in His image, and every neighbour is someone He has redeemed.

He is a God who restores. His justice does not stop at punishing the wrongdoer; it aims at making the victim whole. The thief pays double, fourfold or fivefold, the careless grazier pays "from the best of his own field," verse 5, and even the uncertain case is settled by an oath before the LORD so that trust can be restored, verse 11. God's idea of justice is repair.

He is a God who hears. Few passages in the Law speak of God so personally. "I will surely hear their cry," verse 23; "if he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am compassionate," verse 27. He is the same God who heard Israel groaning in Egypt, Exodus 2:23-24, and the same God before whom the outcry of Sodom rose, Genesis 18:20-21. The cry of the powerless reaches His throne whether any human court listens or not.

He is a God of burning anger against oppression. "My anger will be kindled, and I will kill you with the sword," verse 24. The punishment mirrors the crime: those who prey on widows and orphans will leave widows and orphans behind. God's anger here is not a loss of temper but the settled opposition of love toward whatever crushes the weak. His compassion and His wrath come from the same heart.

He is gracious. The word He uses of Himself in verse 27 is the word He will proclaim on the mountain in Exodus 34:6, "compassionate and gracious." Before Israel ever hears that great self-revelation, it has already heard God describe Himself this way over a poor man's cloak.

He is jealous and holy. He tolerates no sorcery, no other gods, no contempt for His name. He claims the firstfruits of harvest and the firstborn of every family, not because He needs them but because everything is His and Israel lives by His gift. And He calls His people "men of holiness," verse 31, holiness that reaches the kitchen table.

These truths hold together what we often separate. The God who demands exclusive worship is the same God who hears the foreigner's cry. Holiness and compassion are not rival attributes; the holy God is the one most fiercely committed to the weak. For worship, that means our devotion to Him is tested by how we handle money, pledges, debts and the people least able to repay us. "Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender," Proverbs 19:17.

crossReferences.note: Hearing Nathan's parable of the stolen lamb, David pronounces sentence from this chapter's law: "he must pay for the lamb four times over." The king who knew the law well enough to apply it to others had to hear "You are the man," and many readers have heard the fourfold penalty echo through the sorrows that followed in his own family.

Zacchaeus volunteers fourfold restitution, the penalty of Exodus 22:1 for a stolen sheep, treating his tax fraud as theft. Jesus answers, "Today salvation has come to this house." The law's pattern of restitution becomes the fruit of grace rather than the price of it.

Paul goes beyond restitution to transformation. The thief must not only stop stealing and repay; he must work "doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need." The one who took from his neighbour becomes a giver to the poor, the very people Exodus 22:21-27 protects.

Moses grounds the foreigner law in God's character. The "great, mighty, and awesome God" who accepts no bribe "executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing." Israel's care for the stranger imitates what God Himself does, and it remembers Egypt.

The pledge law of Exodus 22:26-27 is developed. A lender must not even enter the borrower's house to choose his pledge, and a poor man's cloak must be returned by sunset "so that he may sleep in his own cloak and bless you." Returning it is "credited to you as righteousness."

The prophet indicts Israel for exactly what this chapter forbids. They sell the needy "for a pair of sandals" and "lie down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge." The cloaks that should have gone home at sunset have become cushions for worship, a devastating picture of religion divorced from justice.

Paul, having rebuked the high priest without knowing who he was, quotes verse 28: "Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people." Even when mistreated by an unjust court, the apostle honours this law, showing that respect for office survives the failures of the office holder.

Jesus tells of a widow who keeps crying for justice until an unjust judge relents. If even he gives in, "Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?" The parable rests on the promise of Exodus 22:23 that God hears the cry of the widow.

James warns rich landowners that "the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts." The language of crying out and being heard is the language of Exodus 22:23 and 27, applied to workers cheated of wages. God's ear for the oppressed has not changed.

The interest law is spelled out further. A countryman who becomes destitute is to be helped "as you would a foreigner or stranger," and no interest or profit may be taken "that your countryman may live among you." The purpose of the loan is his survival, not the lender's gain.

At Nain Jesus meets a widow burying her only son. He has compassion on her, raises the young man, and gives him back to his mother. The God who promised in Exodus 22:23 to hear the widow's cry is present in person, answering it.

Peter applies the call to holiness to the church: "be holy in all you do, for it is written: 'Be holy, because I am holy.'" Like Exodus 22:31, the command reaches into the whole of life, not only worship, and it rests on belonging to the God who redeemed them.

study.oneStory:
God made the world good and gave humanity dominion to cultivate and share it. After the fall, dominion turned to grasping. Cain took his brother's life, and by the time of Exodus a whole empire had turned a guest people into slaves. The story of Scripture is, in part, the story of God reversing that theft.

Exodus 22 comes right after the exodus and the giving of the Ten Commandments. Having brought Israel out of the house of slavery, God now shows what a redeemed community looks like. It is a people in which loss is restored, the thief repays, and the weak are protected because the people remember what it was to be weak themselves. The chapter answers the cry that opened the book: Israel cried out in Egypt, and God heard, Exodus 2:23-24. Now He promises to hear every widow and orphan who cries out within Israel, and to act against Israel if Israel becomes another Egypt.

The rest of the Old Testament shows how often that warning had to be sounded. The prophets used this chapter's triad of foreigner, widow and orphan as the measure of Israel's faithfulness, and the nation's failure to keep it was among the reasons for exile. The law could describe a just community, but it could not produce one.

In Christ the story turns. He is the Son who became poor, the stranger taken in or turned away, the innocent one who repays what He did not steal. Through Him outsiders are brought into God's household, debtors are forgiven, and thieves become givers, Ephesians 4:28. The church is called to be the community this chapter sketched, caring for widows and orphans, lending without exploiting, and living as a holy people in every part of life, James 1:27 and 1 Peter 1:15.

The story ends in a new creation where nothing is stolen and no one is left without a cloak. God Himself "will wipe away every tear," Revelation 21:4, the last cry of the oppressed finally answered. Outside the city are "the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters," Revelation 22:15, the very offences this chapter named as fatal to the covenant. Inside, God's people see His face and serve Him, a holy people at last, and the restitution the law demanded is surpassed by a restoration of all things.

quiz.q: What restitution was required if a man stole and slaughtered an ox, according to verse 1?

options.text: Five oxen for the one ox stolen.
options.note: The text specifies this heavier restitution because the stolen animal could no longer be returned alive.

options.text: A single ox in simple replacement.
options.note: The penalty for slaughtering or selling the stolen ox was heavier than simple replacement, five oxen.

options.text: No restitution was required if the ox was already dead.
options.note: Restitution was explicitly required, and at a multiplied rate for a slaughtered or sold animal.

options.text: The thief's own life was forfeit.
options.note: The penalty specified is restitution in livestock, not the death penalty, for simple theft of this kind.

quiz.q: What warning does God give about mistreating the widow, orphan, or foreigner in verses 22 to 24?

options.text: If they cry out to Him, He will surely hear, and His anger will be kindled against the oppressor.
options.note: This is God's exact, severe warning, tying His personal response to their cry.

options.text: God is indifferent to how the vulnerable are treated.
options.note: The text describes intense divine concern and threatened judgment, the opposite of indifference.

options.text: Only the community's human courts would punish such mistreatment.
options.note: The text frames God's own direct, personal response, not merely human legal process.

options.text: No warning is given regarding this behavior.
options.note: Verses 22 to 24 give an explicit and severe warning.

quiz.q: What restriction does verse 25 place on lending money to a poor Israelite?

options.text: No interest may be charged.
options.note: The text is explicit: you are not to charge him interest, protecting the poor from compounding debt.

options.text: Only very high interest could be charged.
options.note: The text forbids interest altogether in this case, not merely limits it to a high rate.

options.text: Loans to the poor were forbidden entirely.
options.note: Lending itself is assumed and even implicitly encouraged; only interest is forbidden.

options.text: No restriction is placed on lending terms.
options.note: Verse 25 explicitly restricts charging interest to the poor.

quiz.q: What must be done if a neighbor's cloak is taken as collateral, according to verses 26 to 27?

options.text: It must be returned by sunset, since it is his only covering for the night.
options.note: This law protects basic human dignity and physical need even amid a legitimate debt arrangement.

options.text: It may be kept indefinitely until the debt is paid in full.
options.note: The text requires prompt return by sunset regardless of whether the debt itself is settled.

options.text: It must be destroyed rather than returned.
options.note: The text calls for return, not destruction, of the pledged cloak.

options.text: No instruction is given about collateral.
options.note: Verses 26 to 27 give a specific and compassionate instruction about returning collateral.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament echo this chapter's concern for restitution and the vulnerable?

options.text: Zacchaeus promises fourfold restitution after meeting Jesus, and James defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows.
options.note: Luke 19:8 and James 1:27 both directly echo this chapter's central concerns.

options.text: The New Testament shows no interest in restitution or care for the vulnerable.
options.note: Both Luke and James explicitly carry forward exactly these themes.

options.text: Paul explicitly overturns all concern for restitution as legalistic.
options.note: Paul does not reject restitution or care for the vulnerable; these remain consistent New Testament ethical concerns.

options.text: Only the Old Testament addresses these themes; they disappear afterward.
options.note: Luke 19:8 and James 1:27 show clear New Testament continuity with these themes.

questions: Israel's law required restitution that made the wronged party whole, not just punished the offender. When you have wronged someone, do you tend toward genuine restitution or merely feeling bad without concrete repair?

God's warning about the widow, orphan, and foreigner is startlingly personal, 'I will surely hear their cry.' Who in your community is currently crying out in a way you have not yet noticed or responded to?

The law forbade charging interest to a poor neighbor and required returning a pledged cloak by sunset. How does your own use of money reflect, or fail to reflect, this kind of practical compassion for those with less than you?
Zacchaeus responded to grace with immediate, costly restitution. Is there a debt of restitution, financial or relational, that grace is calling you to finally pay?
This whole chapter of civil law is framed by the call, 'you are to be My holy people.' Where do you compartmentalize your faith away from your ordinary financial dealings and everyday disputes?

translationNotes.note: The distinction between a thief killed at night versus after sunrise reflects an ancient legal principle about reasonable use of force in self-defense, presuming greater threat and less certainty of intent in darkness.

Sorceress is feminine in the Hebrew text, though the underlying concern, prohibiting occult practice that claimed power apart from or against the LORD, applied to men and women alike, as parallel laws elsewhere make clear, Deuteronomy 18:10-12.

The command to give the firstborn of sons echoes and assumes the redemption law of Exodus 13:11-15; sons were never to be sacrificed but always redeemed, unlike animals which were consecrated directly.
